title: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES, PROPHESY, UNDERSTAND THE MYSTERIES OF GOD—AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES, PROPHESY, UNDERSTAND THE MYSTERIES OF GOD—AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
The most terrifying spiritual tragedy is not having no gifts from God. It is becoming so impressed with what happens through you that you stop examining what is happening inside you.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.

Not before your pastor. Not before the people who admired your ministry. Not before the thousands who shared your sermons, listened to your prophecies, or testified that your prayers changed their lives.
Before Jesus.
The One who sees what nobody else could see.
And for the first time, there is no microphone to hold. No spiritual language to impress anyone. No ministry title to introduce yourself with. No crowd to confirm how anointed you were.
Only you.
And the Lord who knows you completely.
You begin remembering everything you did in His name.
The prayers. The prophecies. The fasting. The spiritual encounters. The people who called you a mighty man or woman of God.
Surely all of that must mean something.
Then you remember the words Jesus spoke in Matthew 7:22–23.
“Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
And His answer:
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Read those words again.
“I never knew you.”
Not, “You never preached.”
Not, “You never performed impressive works.”
Not even, “You never used My name.”
The warning is far more devastating.
You can be surrounded by religious activity and still be spiritually lost.
You can become familiar with the language of heaven while remaining unwilling to surrender the hidden chambers of your heart.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you might not realize it until everything you trusted to prove your spirituality is exposed as insufficient.
But before you assume this article is about some famous preacher who fell into scandal, some arrogant prophet, or some religious person you know, consider something.
What if the Holy Spirit is asking you to examine yourself?
Not because Jesus wants to destroy you.
But because He loves you too much to let you confuse spiritual performance with a living relationship with Him.
Because there is something more important than being gifted.
Being known by Christ—and belonging to Him.
The apostle Paul understood this danger.
He wrote to a church overflowing with spiritual activity, theological disputes, impressive gifts, and competing claims of spiritual maturity.
The church in Corinth.
These were not people unfamiliar with spiritual gifts.
Paul acknowledged that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift as they waited for Christ's revelation (1 Corinthians 1:7).

Yet this same congregation struggled with division, jealousy, pride, sexual immorality, lawsuits among believers, disorder in worship, and humiliating treatment of poorer members during the Lord's Supper.
They had spiritual gifts.
But their conduct often contradicted the character of the Savior they claimed to follow.
And into that contradiction, Paul spoke words that should still shake the modern church.
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
—1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
The Greek word translated “charity” in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agápē).
Love.
But not merely sentimental affection.
Not simply being polite, agreeable, or emotionally warm.
In Paul's argument, this love expresses itself through patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and concern for the good of others.
It reflects the character of the God who loved us while we were still sinners.
Paul continues:
“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
—1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Nothing.
The Greek expression is οὐθέν εἰμι (outhén eimi).
“I am nothing.”
Paul does not say spiritual gifts are evil.
He does not say prophecy is worthless or that speaking in tongues should be despised.
In fact, he explicitly instructs believers to pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1).
His warning is that gifts without love cannot establish genuine spiritual greatness.
The most impressive manifestation cannot substitute for the character of Christ.
You can speak eloquently about God's holiness while secretly enjoying another person's humiliation.
You can explain the mysteries of Scripture while refusing to forgive someone who wounded your pride.
You can preach repentance to a congregation and spend the evening defending the very sin God has been confronting in your private life.
You can pray loudly in public while refusing to apologize quietly at home.
You can call fire down in your prayers and still have a heart that has grown cold toward the people nearest to you.
And perhaps you have never stood behind a pulpit.
But when someone disagrees with you, something ugly rises inside.
Contempt.
Cruelty.
The satisfaction of making another person look foolish.
And suddenly, the question is no longer whether you know the right verses.
The question is whether those verses have been allowed to confront you.
Because knowing what the Bible says and submitting to what the Bible says are not the same thing.
James warned believers against becoming hearers of the Word without becoming doers (James 1:22).
And Jesus asked a question that still reaches beyond church buildings, denominations, and generations:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
—Luke 6:46, KJV
That question is uncomfortable.
Because it does not allow us to hide behind religious vocabulary.
Jesus is not impressed by the title “Lord” on our lips when our lives persistently refuse His authority.
And this is where we need to be careful.
We must not confuse spiritual gifts with spiritual fruit.
The gifts of the Spirit are discussed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 12.
The fruit of the Spirit is described in Galatians 5:22–23.
Love. Joy. Peace. Longsuffering. Gentleness. Goodness. Faithfulness. Meekness. Temperance.
Gifts are graciously given for service and the building up of Christ's body.
Fruit reflects the Spirit's transforming work in the believer's character.
They are not enemies.
They are not interchangeable.
And neither should be used to replace Jesus Himself.
A person may possess remarkable speaking ability and still be immature.
Someone may demonstrate extraordinary biblical knowledge and still struggle with pride.
A person may be publicly admired for ministry while privately resisting correction.
This does not mean every gifted believer is secretly hypocritical.
It means no believer should mistake giftedness for permission to stop growing in holiness.
The same God who calls us to serve also calls us to repent.
The same Spirit who empowers ministry produces love.
And the same Jesus who sends His people into the world commands them to abide in Him.
Jesus said:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.”
—John 15:4, KJV
The Greek verb translated “abide” is μένω (ménō).
It carries the sense of remaining, continuing, or staying.
Jesus was not describing a momentary emotional experience.
He was describing ongoing dependence upon Him.
A branch does not produce life by announcing how closely connected it is to the vine.
It bears fruit because it remains connected.
And that is where many of us need to examine our hearts.
We have become very good at appearing connected.
We know how to sound spiritual.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to lift our hands when the music reaches its most emotional moment.
But when the music stops, when nobody is watching, when obedience becomes costly, when forgiveness feels unfair, when temptation offers something our flesh desperately wants—
Who are we then?
Not who do we pretend to be.
Who are we becoming?
There is a kind of religious life that can become an elaborate hiding place.
A man may lead powerful prayers at church while his wife quietly cries because he refuses to listen to her.
A woman may encourage hundreds of strangers online while carrying bitterness she refuses to bring before God.
A ministry leader may preach against greed while privately measuring every relationship by what it can contribute to his platform.
A Bible teacher may explain grace beautifully while showing none to the person who made an honest mistake.
And someone reading this may be thinking:
“I used to be different.”
You remember when you first encountered the mercy of Jesus.
You did not care whether anyone noticed your prayers.
You were simply grateful that God heard them.
You did not need a title.
You were amazed to be forgiven.
You did not measure your spiritual life by influence.
You measured your days by how desperately you needed the Savior.
Somewhere along the way, perhaps the work of ministry became louder than the voice of the Master.
You started protecting an image instead of confessing your struggles.
You learned how to speak about brokenness without admitting your own.
You became afraid that if people saw your weakness, they would stop respecting you.
So you kept serving.
Kept posting.
Kept preaching.
Kept smiling.
While something inside you was quietly starving.
And now the question you are afraid to ask is rising again.
Have I been doing things for Jesus while drifting away from Jesus?
There is a moment in Luke 10 that speaks powerfully to this fear.
Jesus sent out seventy disciples, according to the traditional Greek text reflected in the King James Version. Some ancient manuscripts read seventy-two.
They returned rejoicing that even demons were subject to them through His name.
Imagine their excitement.
They had witnessed extraordinary spiritual authority.
But Jesus redirected their joy.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.”
—Luke 10:20, KJV
What a correction.
Jesus did not deny the reality of what they had experienced.
He redirected them toward a greater reason for rejoicing.
Not spiritual power.
Not public success.
Not supernatural experiences.
But their standing before God.
Your deepest joy must never rest in how much spiritual power people believe you possess.
It must rest in the saving grace of God.
And if that truth does not humble us, we have not understood it deeply enough.
Because salvation is not an achievement we present to Jesus.
It is mercy we receive through Him.
Paul wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
—Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (cháris).
God's gracious favor and gift.
We are not saved because our sermons were powerful.
Not because our prayers sounded impressive.
Not because we accumulated enough spiritual accomplishments.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the very next verse teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Good works matter.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
Love matters.
But they are not the price by which we purchase salvation.
They are part of the life God creates in those who belong to Christ.
This distinction is everything.
Because without it, a message about love can become another exhausting attempt to earn God's acceptance.
You begin thinking you must become perfectly patient before Jesus will receive you.
Perfectly gentle before you can approach Him.
Perfectly pure before you can ask for forgiveness.
But the Gospel does not tell sinners to repair themselves and then approach the Savior.
It calls sinners to repent and believe in the Savior who died and rose again.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him (Titus 2:11–14).
Consider Peter.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Quick to speak.
He confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).
He witnessed the transfiguration.
He walked on water toward Jesus.
He promised loyalty even unto death.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke records that after Peter's third denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
—Luke 22:62, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The man who had spoken so confidently about his devotion was suddenly confronted with his own weakness.
His words had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
And the Savior he had promised never to abandon was being led toward suffering.
What could Peter possibly say?
What explanation would make his denial acceptable?
There was none.
Only tears.
Only failure.
Only the terrible realization that he was not as strong as he believed.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias.
And in John 21, Jesus asked Peter a question.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Not, “Peter, how many people will follow your ministry?”
Not, “Peter, can you explain every mystery?”
Not, “Peter, can you prove how powerful you are?”
“Lovest thou me?”
Three times, Jesus questioned Peter about his love, and three times Peter responded.

The exchange is rich with meaning, but we should avoid a popular oversimplification: although the Greek text uses both ἀγαπάω (agapáō) and φιλέω (philéō), John's Gospel sometimes uses these verbs interchangeably. We cannot confidently build the entire meaning of Peter's restoration upon a supposed sharp contrast between two different levels of love.
What the passage clearly reveals is more than enough.
The risen Christ confronted the disciple who had denied Him.
And He restored Peter to the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
“Feed my sheep.”
—John 21:17, KJV
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
Christ's mercy was greater.
And the restoration did not end with a comforting conversation.
Jesus called Peter to follow Him, even along a path that would involve suffering.
Grace was not permission to return to self-confidence.
Grace was an invitation into renewed obedience.
That is the Gospel.
Not the denial of sin.
Not the celebration of scandal.
Not the claim that consequences never matter.
But the breathtaking truth that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You may have been spiritually proud.
You may have confused ministry success with intimacy with God.
You may have wounded people while claiming to defend the truth.
You may have used your knowledge of Scripture to win arguments rather than love your neighbor.
You may have been hiding behind your reputation because admitting your sin feels unbearable.
But if the Lord is exposing your heart through His Word, do not waste that mercy by defending yourself.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness from those you have wronged.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
Turn away from what is destroying your fellowship with God and harming others.
And come to Jesus.
Not with a résumé.
Not with a list of spiritual achievements.
Not with a carefully prepared explanation of why your behavior was understandable.
Come with empty hands.
Because the hands that were pierced for sinners are more than sufficient to receive those who turn to Him.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
The Greek verb translated “confess,” ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), is a form of ὁμολογέω (homologéō), meaning to acknowledge or confess.
Confession is not merely feeling embarrassed that we were caught.
It is agreeing with the truth about our sin before God.
No more disguising pride as discernment.
No more calling cruelty boldness.
No more confusing attention with anointing.
No more treating ministry activity as a substitute for private obedience.
No more pretending that because God has used us, He must approve of everything we do.
And no more believing that our failures are beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
There is room at the cross for repentant sinners.
But there is no room at the cross for boasting.
And this is why 1 Corinthians 13 is so much more than a beautiful passage read at weddings.
It is a confrontation.
A mirror.
A summons to become more like Jesus.
“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.”
—1 Corinthians 13:4, KJV
Read that slowly.
Love is patient.
When someone disappoints you.
Love is kind.
When you have enough information to humiliate someone but choose to speak truth without cruelty.
Love does not envy.
When another person's ministry grows faster than yours.
Love does not boast.
When God gives you opportunities others may never receive.
Love is not arrogant.
When you know more Scripture than the person asking a sincere question.
Love rejoices in the truth.
Even when the truth exposes your own sin.
Love does not excuse evil or demand silence from those who have been harmed. Biblical love stands with truth, protects the vulnerable, and refuses to use spiritual language to conceal wrongdoing.
And above all, biblical love is not merely an ideal we admire.
It is displayed supremely in Jesus Christ.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who touched the unclean.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who spoke with uncompromising truth to religious hypocrites.
The One who willingly laid down His life.
Paul declared:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
That is the love we are called to reflect.
Not a manufactured sweetness that refuses to confront sin.
Not a performative kindness designed to earn applause.
Not an emotional experience that disappears when obedience becomes difficult.
Christlike love is grounded in truth, shaped by holiness, and sustained by grace.
It costs something.
Sometimes it costs your pride.
Sometimes it costs your reputation.
Sometimes it costs the satisfaction of winning an argument.
Sometimes it requires you to say three words your ego has been resisting for years.
“I was wrong.”
Or four words that might begin a long-overdue healing process.
“Will you forgive me?”
Perhaps the person who needs to hear those words is sitting in the same house as you.
Perhaps your children know how passionately you worship but rarely experience your gentleness.
Perhaps your spouse has heard you speak beautifully about grace while waiting years to receive an apology.
Perhaps someone left the church wounded by the way you treated them, and you have been calling their departure rebellion because admitting your responsibility would be painful.
If this is exposing something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Sit with the question.
What is the Holy Spirit calling you to surrender?
Not to impress anyone with a public confession.
Not to reveal private sins that should be addressed safely and appropriately.
But as a simple acknowledgment that you want the truth of Christ to reach beyond your outward appearance.
There are believers who need to know they are not the only ones struggling.
And sometimes a humble request for prayer is the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
But do not stop at a comment.
Let the conviction become obedience.
Let the prayer become repentance.
Let the repentance produce fruit.
Because Jesus is not calling us to perform vulnerability for an audience.
He is calling us to follow Him.
There is another warning in Paul's words that we cannot afford to ignore.
“And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
—1 Corinthians 13:3, KJV
Even extraordinary sacrifice can be corrupted by the wrong motives.
A person may give generously and still crave admiration.
A ministry may accomplish visible good while its leaders neglect humility and accountability.
A Christian may sacrifice time, money, and comfort while secretly believing those sacrifices make them superior to others.
And it is why financial generosity must never be presented as a way to purchase God's favor.
Jesus does not sell salvation.
The Holy Spirit is not a reward for financial contributions.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not coerced.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek word ἀνάγκη (anánkē), translated “necessity,” can convey compulsion or constraint.
Paul's instruction protects the freedom and sincerity of Christian generosity.

So if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, recognize hidden sin, rediscover the mercy of Jesus, or grow in your walk with Christ, there is a meaningful opportunity to help carry that work further.
Not because financial support guarantees spiritual blessing.
But because you freely believe that Scripture-centered encouragement, Gospel proclamation, and discipleship resources are worth helping others receive.
What matters is that the decision comes from faith, wisdom, genuine willingness, and love.
And there is something beautiful about knowing that a resource which strengthened you today might reach someone tomorrow who is quietly losing hope.
Someone sitting alone after a terrible mistake.
Someone afraid to return to church.
Someone convinced that their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has never truly understood why Jesus died on the cross.
Someone who needs to discover that repentance is not the end of their story.
Christ is.
These resources are part of a wider mission to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford paid materials.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or promises of divine favor.
The greater purpose remains the same.
To make much of Jesus.
To help people encounter the truth of Scripture.
To encourage genuine repentance, lasting discipleship, and lives increasingly transformed by the grace of God.
You can still help.
Not merely to increase a page's reach, but because someone among your friends may need its message.
A person who has spent years mistaking religious activity for a relationship with Jesus.
A believer who has grown weary of pretending.
A ministry worker who needs to rediscover the joy of simply belonging to Christ.
A friend who has wandered far from God and no longer believes restoration is possible.
But never forget this.
The mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
If a ministry becomes more concerned with its own influence than with faithfulness to Christ, it has lost sight of its calling.
If a Christian becomes more interested in being admired than in being transformed, something is terribly wrong.
And if we preach grace to the world but refuse to extend grace to repentant people, we contradict the very Gospel we claim to defend.
The church does not need more spiritual celebrities.
It needs disciples who love Jesus.
It needs believers who will speak truth without arrogance.
People who will serve when nobody applauds.
People who will confess sin without manufacturing excuses.
People who will protect the vulnerable rather than defend wrongdoing for the sake of a ministry's reputation.
People who will open their Bibles not merely to prepare another post, but to hear and obey the Lord.
People who understand that the purpose of spiritual gifts is not self-exaltation but service.
People who remember that the greatest commandment is to love God with all their heart, soul, and mind, and the second is to love their neighbor as themselves (Matthew 22:37–39).
And above all, people who understand that their hope rests not in their own greatness but in the crucified and risen Christ.
There is a reason Paul could write so powerfully about love.
His own life had been radically interrupted by grace.
Before becoming an apostle, Paul persecuted the church of God.
He knew what it meant to be religiously zealous and tragically wrong.
He knew Scripture.
He had convictions.
He believed he was defending what was holy.
Yet he was opposing the very Messiah whom the Scriptures proclaimed.
Then the risen Jesus confronted him.
And the persecutor became a servant of the One he had persecuted.
Paul would later write:
—1 Corinthians 15:10, KJV
Not by his intellectual brilliance.
Not by his religious credentials.
Not by his impressive accomplishments.
By the grace of God.
That is the confession every believer must return to.
The preacher.
The worship leader.
The prophet.
The teacher.
The new Christian.
The exhausted parent.
The person who has served faithfully for decades.
The person who has just returned to church after years of running.
We stand in need of the same Savior.
And the Gospel is not that spiritually impressive people finally become worthy of God's attention.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is not merely a moral example.
He is the Savior and Lord.
And through Him, sinners are called to repent, believe, receive forgiveness, and walk in newness of life.
That is why the words “I never knew you” should not drive us toward frantic attempts to manufacture spiritual achievements.
They should drive us toward Jesus Himself.
Toward genuine faith.
Toward repentance.
Toward obedience that flows from grace.
Toward the love that the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ.
Because on the day we stand before Him, no number of followers can save us.
No ministry title can justify us.
No record of religious accomplishments can take the place of His righteousness.
Our only sufficient hope is Jesus Christ.
And those who truly belong to Him are called to follow Him.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
Not whether people think you are spiritual.
Not whether you can quote more verses than someone else.
Not whether your prayers move a congregation.
Not whether your posts receive thousands of reactions.
Ask yourself:
Am I trusting in Jesus Christ, and is His grace changing the way I live and love?
If the answer exposes something painful, do not despair.
The purpose of conviction is not to leave the repentant sinner hopeless.
It is to bring what is hidden into the light of God's truth.
You can turn to Christ today.
You can ask Him for mercy.
You can begin making things right.
You can stop defending the sin that has been destroying you.
You can ask trusted believers to walk with you in accountability and prayer.
And if you have fallen, you do not have to pretend that the fall never happened in order to seek restoration.
Jesus knows the truth already.
Come to Him with it.
“Christ is still healing me.”
And if you are struggling to believe that restoration is possible, write:
Not as a declaration of confidence in your own strength, but as a prayerful acknowledgment that you are looking to Christ and refusing to abandon the hope of His Gospel.
Let others pray with you.
Let the Word confront you.
Let grace humble you.
And let love become more than something you preach.
Let it become something people experience when they encounter your life.
Because the world has heard enough Christians proclaim that God is love while treating people as though love were optional.
May they see something different in us.
May they see truth with compassion.
Conviction with humility.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
Courage without cruelty.
Repentance without excuses.
Grace without compromise.
And through all of it, may they see Jesus.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who calls His people to obedience.
The Shepherd who restores the wandering.
The King who will one day make all things new.
You may speak in tongues.
You may prophesy.
You may understand mysteries.
You may have faith that astonishes people.
But do not let the extraordinary things you do distract you from the extraordinary Savior you need.
Paul ends his great chapter on love with these words:
“And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”
—1 Corinthians 13:13, KJV
Faith.
Hope.
Love.
And the greatest is love.
Not because love replaces the Gospel.
But because the Gospel reveals the love of God in Jesus Christ and calls His redeemed people to live in that love.
When the applause fades, when the platform disappears, when every hidden motive stands exposed before the Lord, may our hope be found in Christ alone.
And may the love He has shown us be visible in the lives we have surrendered to Him.

The greatest tragedy is not reaching the end of your life without the world knowing your name—it is spending your life making a name for yourself while never truly surrendering to the One who died to save you.
